nameStory: The spotted trunkfish gets its name from the distinctive black spots scattered across its body, which look like polka dots on a gift box. The 'trunk' part comes from its rigid, box-like body shape that resembles a small treasure chest or trunk, making it one of the most uniquely shaped fish in the ocean.
description: The spotted trunkfish is a remarkable box-shaped fish with a hard, bony exterior that acts like natural armor. Its body is whitish to golden-yellow with distinctive black spots dotting the surface, and it has a triangular profile when viewed from the front. This tropical visitor is typically small to medium-sized and moves through the water with an adorable wiggling motion using just its fins, since its rigid body can't bend like other fish.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Unmistakable box-like body that feels hard and bony to the touch, like tapping on a small wooden crate - completely rigid with no flexibility

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Whitish to golden-yellow background decorated with distinct black spots of varying sizes, creating a polka-dot pattern that's easy to spot underwater

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Small, constantly fluttering fins that do all the work of propulsion since the body is too rigid to help with swimming - watch for the characteristic wiggling motion

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, protruding mouth positioned at the front tip of the triangular face, perfect for picking at small prey items

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Typically found around coral reefs and rocky structures in warm, tropical waters - extremely rare in New England waters

habitat: The spotted trunkfish is not a native New England species and has only been recorded once in our region's waters. It normally lives in warm Caribbean coral reefs and would only appear here as an extremely rare vagrant, possibly carried north by warm Gulf Stream currents during unusual oceanographic conditions.

seasonality.spring: Any sighting would be exceptionally rare, but slightly more possible as Gulf Stream currents strengthen and could carry tropical strays northward.
seasonality.summer: The only season when water temperatures might briefly support a tropical vagrant, though survival would be unlikely in New England's cooler waters.
seasonality.fall: Extremely unlikely to be seen as water temperatures begin dropping below what this tropical species can tolerate.
seasonality.winter: Impossible to find, as the cold New England waters would be lethal to this warm-water species.

funFact: When threatened, spotted trunkfish can release a toxic slime from their skin that's so potent it can kill other fish in the same aquarium tank - they're literally swimming chemical weapons factories!
confusionNotes: In the extremely unlikely event you see one in New England waters, it could only be confused with its relative the buffalo trunkfish, but the spotted trunkfish has distinct black spots while the buffalo trunkfish has a more mottled, honeycomb-like pattern without clear spots.
contextualKnowledge: This fish is known by many names in the Caribbean including boxfish, cow-fish, and shellfish, which can be confusing since it's not actually related to cows or shellfish. The single New England sighting represents an extraordinary vagrant occurrence, making any local observation scientifically significant.
compareHints: The spotted trunkfish differs from its close relative the buffalo trunkfish by having distinct black spots rather than a honeycomb or net-like pattern. Both share the same rigid, box-like body shape and small wiggling fins, but the spotted trunkfish typically has a cleaner white-to-yellow background color that makes its spots stand out more prominently.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Buffalo Trunkfish differs from its relative the Spotted Trunkfish by having a more triangular (rather than rounded) cross-section when viewed head-on, and typically shows more geometric patterns rather than simple spots.
